stated_availability: Section 4.2/Results (p. 7): "We used the IntCal20 curve for all models (Reimer et al., 2020) using the calibration process defined in equation [3]. All data and R scripts are available on https://github.com/ercrema/diffusionCurve and permanently archived on https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10782942." Also, Appendix A (p. 9): "Supplementary data to this article can be found online at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jas.2024.105962." Article licence (p. 1): "This is an open access article under the CC BY license (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)" — article-scoped; no licence is stated for the GitHub/Zenodo deposit. (Descriptive only; not mapped to L1-L6.)

F1.evidence: Zenodo DOI given for the deposited data: "All data and R scripts are available on https://github.com/ercrema/diffusionCurve and permanently archived on https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10782942" (p. 7). A DOI is a globally unique persistent identifier (instrument F1: DOI).

F2.evidence: Deposit is on Zenodo, which mints DataCite metadata (mandatory creators, title, publisher, publication year, resource type, description) for every record; the paper's Materials section additionally supplies a structured description of the datasets (n = 551 dates from 215 sites for Japan; n = 928 from 314 sites for Britain; n = 1417 cremation and n = 1119 inhumation dates, pp. 5).

F3.evidence: The DataCite record for a Zenodo deposit carries the DOI in its Identifier field, and the paper's availability statement binds the identifier to the resource: "permanently archived on https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10782942" (p. 7).

F4.evidence: Deposited in Zenodo, named explicitly in the instrument as a qualifying searchable registry (F4: "Zenodo, CRAN, DataCite"); Zenodo records are indexed via DataCite and OpenAIRE. GitHub mirror at https://github.com/ercrema/diffusionCurve provides secondary discovery.

A1.evidence: Retrievable via DOI resolution over HTTPS (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10782942) plus HTTPS from GitHub. Completeness rule satisfied: coverage_category is "substantial" (16/18 datasets Tier 0-2, 88.9%), because the analysis-ready compilations for all three case studies and the three simulated datasets are stated to be in the deposit; only two upstream literature sources (Healy 2012 Oxbow chapter; Willis 2021 BAR monograph) are Tier 3.

A1_1.evidence: Access is via open, free, universally implementable protocols — DOI/HTTPS resolution to Zenodo and HTTPS to GitHub; no login, subscription, or proprietary client is required ("All data and R scripts are available on https://github.com/ercrema/diffusionCurve", p. 7).

A1_2.evidence: HTTPS/DOI resolution supports authentication and authorisation where necessary; here no restriction is necessary and the data are openly deposited, so the "where needed" condition is met trivially. No ethical or CARE-based restriction is invoked in the paper (radiocarbon determinations on plant remains and cremated/inhumed burial contexts, pp. 5).

A2.evidence: Zenodo (CERN-operated) commits to metadata persistence with DataCite tombstone records even if files are withdrawn; the deposit is described by the authors as "permanently archived" (p. 7), unlike the GitHub copy alone.

I1.evidence: The deposited data are consumed directly by the archived R scripts implementing the NIMBLE models ("Both the hierarchical model described in equations [5-6] and the random walk ICAR model were implemented using the NIMBLE ... probabilistic programming language in R", p. 5-6), which entails machine-parseable tabular/serialised formats (not PDF or Word tables); radiocarbon records are structured as 14C age plus error fields per equation [4] (p. 2).

I2.evidence: No controlled vocabulary, ontology, gazetteer, or thesaurus with PIDs is cited for periods, places, taxa, or site types (no PeriodO, Pleiades, Getty AAT, CIDOC-CRM, or ARIADNEplus vocabulary anywhere in Materials and methods, pp. 5-6, or the availability statement, p. 7). Chronological terms ("Late Neolithic", "Middle Bronze Age") and taxon names are used as free text.

I3.evidence: Upstream sources are cited only as prose literature references ("Japanese dates were collated from ... databases of Japan (Kudo et al., 2023)"; "Radiocarbon dates from Britain were obtained from Bevan et al. (2017)"; case study 2 "collated from different published sources", p. 5). These are untyped, human-readable citations rather than PID-based qualified links in the dataset's own metadata; several sources (Healy 2012, Willis 2021, Bloxam 2020, Wilkin 2013) have no PID at all. No relatedIdentifier assertions are evidenced from the paper.

R1.evidence: Rich description of the data in section 4.1: counts and provenance ("a total of 1479 14C dates on seed remains from Japan (n = 551, from 215 sites ...) and Britain (n = 928, from 314 sites)"), taxa (rice n = 203; wild nuts n = 348; wheat n = 261; barley n = 130; hazelnut n = 537), chronological windows, geographic exclusions (Hokkaido and the Ryukyus), and spatial coverage mapped in Fig. 1 (pp. 5).

R1_1.evidence: No usage licence is stated for the deposited data. The only licence statements are article-scoped: "This is an open access article under the CC BY license" (p. 1) and "the author has applied a Creative Commons Attribution (CC BY) licence to any Author Accepted Manuscript version arising from this submission" (p. 9). Per the PID guide's three-way distinction, licence status for the Zenodo/GitHub deposit is "unclear" (not stated in the paper), which does not meet R1.1; the instrument scores evidenced practice and unscoreable sub-principles score 0.

R1_2.evidence: Detailed provenance: named source databases and publications for every case study, plus explicit derivation and filtering steps — "We considered dates with a cumulative calibrated probability mass equal to or larger than 0.5 for the interval 4000-1700 cal BP"; "We filtered the initial dataset considering dates with a cumulative calibrated probability ... for the interval 7000-3000 cal BP"; "We used a higher probability threshold (0.99 instead of 0.5) to avoid any edge effects caused by the ICAR model" (p. 5); calibration provenance via IntCal20 (Reimer et al., 2020, p. 7).

R1_3.evidence: Data conform to radiocarbon community reporting and processing conventions: uncalibrated determinations with measurement error handled per equation [4] ("σi is the square root of the sum of the squares of the sample 14C age error and the corresponding error in the calibration curve", p. 2), calibration against the community-standard IntCal20 curve (p. 7), and site-level attribution enabling the site random effect kj; deposit carries DataCite metadata, listed in the guide as a qualifying community standard.

F1.evidence: The same Zenodo DOI covers the analysis code: "All data and R scripts are available on https://github.com/ercrema/diffusionCurve and permanently archived on https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10782942" (p. 7) — an archival DOI, not a bare GitHub URL.

F2.evidence: Zenodo deposit generates DataCite metadata automatically (creators, title, publisher, year, resource type, description); the paper further identifies the software stack and version: "the nimbleCarbon R package (Crema, 2022b)" with reference "nimbleCarbon: Models and Utility Functions for Bayesian Analyses of Radiocarbon Dates with NIMBLE, 0.2.0" (pp. 6, 10).

F3.evidence: The archival DOI is the identifier of the code record itself and is stated in the availability sentence: "permanently archived on https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10782942" (p. 7); Zenodo/DataCite records embed the DOI in their metadata.

F4.evidence: Code archived in Zenodo — explicitly named in the instrument's F4 examples — and therefore indexed via DataCite/OpenAIRE; live repository additionally discoverable at https://github.com/ercrema/diffusionCurve (p. 7).

A1.evidence: Source code retrievable by its identifier over HTTPS via DOI resolution to Zenodo, with a public GitHub mirror; no request-based or gated access (p. 7).

A1_1.evidence: HTTPS/DOI resolution is open, free, and universally implementable; the code is plain R source requiring only open-source R and NIMBLE ("implemented using the NIMBLE ... probabilistic programming language in R (R Core Team, 2020)", pp. 5-6) — no proprietary runtime or licensed software.

A1_2.evidence: Retrieval protocol (HTTPS) supports authentication/authorisation where needed; none is needed here as the repository and archive are fully open, and no restriction on the code is asserted anywhere in the paper.

A2.evidence: Zenodo's DataCite metadata persists independently of file availability (tombstone records); the authors distinguish the live GitHub repository from the archive that is "permanently archived" (p. 7), so metadata survives loss of the GitHub copy.

I1.evidence: Code is written in R, an open, formal, widely implemented language, using the open NIMBLE probabilistic programming framework and the nimbleCarbon package (pp. 5-6); scripts are plain-text and machine-executable rather than narrative descriptions or binaries.

I2.evidence: No software metadata vocabulary or standard is evidenced — no CodeMeta.json, CITATION.cff, or controlled vocabulary is mentioned in the availability statement (p. 7) or anywhere in the paper; dependency semantics are conveyed only through prose citation.

I3.evidence: Dependencies are referenced as qualified, PID-bearing relations of the "uses software [DOI]" type: NIMBLE cited with its archival DOI ("de Valpine, P., et al., 2020. NIMBLE: MCMC, Particle Filtering, and Programmable Hierarchical Modeling. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.1211190", p. 10), nimbleCarbon with version 0.2.0 (p. 10), R Core Team (2020), and the IntCal20 calibration curve (Reimer et al., 2020) named as the curve "used ... for all models" (p. 7).

R1.evidence: Analysis is richly documented for reuse: prior specifications ("r ~ Exponential(100)", "mu ~ Beta(2,2)", "phi ~ Gamma(5,0.1)"), truncated normal prior on m with stated means/SDs, and full MCMC settings ("four chains, each with 1 million iterations (half discarded as burn-in) and with thinning set to 50"; ICAR: "four chains, each with 100,000 iterations (20,000 of which were discarded for burn-in), with parameters collected every four steps"), plus convergence diagnostics (Gelman-Rubin, agreement indices) (p. 6).

R1_1.evidence: No code licence is stated. The paper's only licence statements cover the article and the Author Accepted Manuscript ("This is an open access article under the CC BY license", p. 1; "the author has applied a Creative Commons Attribution (CC BY) licence to any Author Accepted Manuscript version", p. 9), not the GitHub/Zenodo scripts. Licence status for the code artefact is unclear from the sole paper source, so R1.1 is unscoreable and scores 0.

R1_2.evidence: Provenance of the computational workflow is documented: version-controlled GitHub repository plus a permanent archived snapshot (p. 7), named software with version (nimbleCarbon 0.2.0; NIMBLE; R Core Team 2020, pp. 6, 10), model equations [5]-[9] mapped to the fitted models, and simulation parameter settings ("r = 0.01, m = 2900 BP, mu = 0.65, phi = 50 (simulation 1a); and r = 0.008, m = 4500 BP, mu = 0.8, phi = 40 (simulation 1b)", p. 5).

R1_3.evidence: Meets computational-archaeology community standards for reproducibility (Marwick 2017): open R code deposited on GitHub with a Zenodo archival DOI, built on CRAN-ecosystem packages, and independently checked — "We thank ... Ben Marwick for reviewing the computational code and providing suggestions to improve its reproducibility" (Acknowledgements, p. 9). Deposit carries DataCite metadata.

closed monograph: Willis, C., 2021, 'Stonehenge and Middle to Late Neolithic Cremation Rites in Mainland Britain', BAR British Series — a source for the case study 2 burial dates (Tier 3)

paywall / manual PDF extraction required for several upstream burial-date sources (Bloxam and Parker Pearson 2022, Proc. Prehist. Soc.; Willis et al. 2016, Antiquity; Olalde et al. 2018 Nature supplementary tables) — Tier 2
institutional-repository doctoral theses requiring manual extraction (Bloxam 2020, UCL; Wilkin 2013, University of Birmingham) — Tier 2

mitigating factor: the analysis-ready compilations for all three case studies, the three simulated datasets, and the R scripts are stated to be deposited (Zenodo DOI 10.5281/zenodo.10782942), so upstream Tier 2-3 barriers do not block reproduction of the reported analyses
no ethical or CARE-based restrictions are invoked; the two Tier 3 items are commercial-publication barriers, not ethics restrictions
